public_rationale: The main factual claim holds. Crunchbase found global venture funding in Q1 2023 was $76 billion, down 53% from $162 billion a year earlier (e1). CB Insights found $58.6 billion, the latest drop in a run of quarterly declines (e2). Investors still held record unspent funds (e4), so the money was there but not being deployed. On the second clause, the checkable part also fits: AI was the 'bright spot' and took about 19% of Q1 dollars, led by OpenAI's $10 billion round (e3). But most money still went elsewhere, so this holds as a tilt, not as all new investment. His claim about what investors 'want' is a hedged reading of intent and is not scored here.
limitations: The outcome rests on the funding decline and a modest reading of the AI tilt. Investor intent to automate labor is not graded.
AI's 19% share means most Q1 2023 dollars went to non-AI companies, and Stripe's round was the second-largest deal.
Tracker totals differ (Crunchbase $76B, CB Insights $58.6B), though both show a clear decline.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: People with money are investing less than they used to, and what they do invest goes into things that suggest they want to try to automate away labor.
conditions: suggest that they want to try

statement.excerpt: The people with the money are not investing it as much as they used to, and when they do, they are investing it in things that suggest that they want to try and automate away labor.

from_speaker: are not investing it as much as they used to
when they do, they are investing it in things
that suggest that they want to try and automate away labor
context: venture capital, generative AI, early 2023
our_interpretation: 'The people with the money' means venture and growth investors in startups, as the surrounding paragraphs about venture capital make clear.

'Not investing it as much as they used to' is read as: venture funding deployed around the post date was clearly lower than in the recent boom (2021 to early 2022). No threshold was given, so any large and clear drop counts.
He described an ongoing state without naming a period. I use the latest quarter public data could report on before the post: Q1 2023 (January to March 2023).

The second clause is hedged: the deals 'suggest' investors 'want to try' to automate labor. That is his reading of investor intent, and it is not scored. Following the reviewers' note, I do not try to prove or disprove intent with evidence about task automation.

The factual core of the second clause that can be checked is narrow: the money that was invested leaned noticeably toward AI (the post frames generative AI as the job-taking technology). This is checked only as a secondary point, and 'when they do' is not read as 'all of it'.
criteria.support_condition: Venture-data trackers show Q1 2023 global venture funding well below the year-earlier or 2021 levels, and AI stands out as a growing or favored area of the money that was invested.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Trackers show Q1 2023 venture funding flat or up versus 2021 or early 2022 levels, or show AI getting a small or falling share of investment.

evidence.excerpt: Global funding in the first quarter reached $76 billion — marking a 53% decline year over year from $162 billion in the first quarter of 2022.
evidence.explanation: Global venture funding in Q1 2023 was about half the year-earlier level. That supports 'not investing it as much as they used to.'

evidence.excerpt: Global venture funding reached $58.6B in Q1’23, a 13% drop quarter-over-quarter (QoQ).
evidence.explanation: A second tracker shows Q1 2023 funding falling for a further quarter after big drops in Q3 and Q4 2022. Its headline calls this a slide to pre-pandemic levels.

evidence.excerpt: But artificial intelligence remains a bright spot, with large fundings in Q1 2023. Companies tagged with AI accounted for 19% of investment dollars last quarter
evidence.explanation: While overall funding fell, AI was the stand-out area and took nearly one in five dollars. That fits the checkable core of the second clause. It also shows most money still went elsewhere, so 'when they do' holds only as a tilt, not as all of it.
